name: Groupthink
statement: Cohesive, insulated groups under a directive leader are said to suppress doubt and choose badly, a chain Turner and Pratkanis found no research had supported end to end.
meaning: Janis's claim is a chain, not an observation. Certain conditions come first: a cohesive group, insulation from outside experts, a leader who signals a preferred answer, no method for weighing options, members alike in background and under stress. Those conditions are said to produce a drive for concurrence. Concurrence seeking then produces the symptoms the name is famous for. Janis's 1972 text names eight of them: an illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalisation, belief in the group's inherent morality, stereotyped views of enemy leaders, direct pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, a shared illusion of unanimity, and self-appointed mindguards. The symptoms in turn produce what Janis called at least six major defects in decision-making, among them a discussion limited to a few options, no reappraisal of the preferred course, and no attempt to get estimates from experts. Those defects produce the fiasco. Each link is separately testable. The part that made the theory interesting is the first link, because the later ones say that bad procedure makes bad decisions, which few people dispute.

origin.where: the book Victims of Groupthink: A Psychological Study of Foreign-Policy Decisions and Fiascoes (Houghton Mifflin)
origin.note: The evidence was a set of qualitative readings of American policy decisions. The preface names four fiascoes given intensive case study, the failure to prepare for Pearl Harbor, the invasion of North Korea, the Bay of Pigs and the escalation of Vietnam, and two contrasting cases of careful decision, the Cuban missile crisis and the Marshall Plan. Janis writes that the case studies rest mainly on secondary sources, memoirs and published documents, and that the book belongs to the stage of hypothesis construction. A revised second edition appeared in 1982 as Groupthink: Psychological Studies of Policy Decisions and Fiascoes. Tetlock and colleagues worked from six groupthink cases in that edition, the Chamberlain cabinet, Admiral Kimmel's command, the Truman cabinet, the Kennedy cabinet over the Bay of Pigs, Johnson's Tuesday Lunch Group and the Nixon Watergate group, against the two vigilant cases. Chamberlain and Watergate are not among the 1972 case studies.

evidence: Janis worked backwards from outcomes he already knew were bad, reading histories of each group for the symptoms his model named. He said as much. His conclusion states that until the account is supported by controlled experiments and systematic correlational research, as well as by case studies, any prescriptions drawn from it are speculative inferences. No group was measured before its decision, and no comparison group was sampled at random. Turner and Pratkanis, introducing a special issue on the model's first 25 years, count fewer than two dozen empirical investigations in that period. That is roughly one a year, against the volume of work on cognitive dissonance or attribution over the same span. They also separate three readings of the theory. A strict reading requires all the antecedent conditions to be present. An additive reading makes groupthink more pronounced as more antecedents accumulate. A liberal reading lets the outcome depend on which particular antecedents are in play. Of the first two they write that no published studies provide evidence for either. On the chain as a whole their verdict is flat: no research has supported the hypothesised links among the five antecedents, the seven groupthink symptoms and the eight defective decision making symptoms. Those two counts are theirs, not Janis's, and the 1972 book gives eight symptoms and six defects. Esser's review of the same 25 years is titled 'Alive and Well'. Its abstract claims considerable heuristic value for the model and a small but growing body of empirical literature. The sentence usually quoted against Esser, that the small number of laboratory tests is not enough to evaluate each antecedent let alone the complete theory, is reproduced by Baron from page 133 and does not appear in the abstract. Park's earlier review reached the same place from the other side, finding few empirical studies of groupthink alongside many criticisms of it, and faulting those studies for testing a limited set of the model's variables. Henningsen and colleagues later turned an experiment on the method rather than the model. Their abstract argues that the symptoms reflect two processes rather than one, and that qualitative work can manufacture a correlation among the symptoms through retrospective sensemaking once people know the decision went badly.

replication.headline: Independent historians describe Janis's cases much as he did, and the antecedent conditions that were supposed to cause the trouble do not predict it.
replication.detail: Tetlock, Peterson, McGuire, Chang and Feld ran the closest thing to a repeat of the original. Nine graduate students and postdoctoral fellows read independent historical sources on the same groups and rated them with a 100-item Q sort. Two observers read each source, one of them always unaware of the hypotheses. The result was 88 Q sorts across 10 decision episodes. The descriptive part held. Q sorts drawn from other historians correlated with Q sorts drawn from Janis's own accounts at .60 on average, from .47 for the Nixon Watergate group to .81 for the Kennedy missile crisis group, with .75 for the Kennedy cabinet over the Bay of Pigs. The causal part did not. In their strictly defined Janis model the path from structural and procedural faults of the organisation to concurrence seeking was .82, and the paths onward to symptoms and to defective decision making were .70 and .87. The paths from group cohesiveness and from provocative situational context to concurrence seeking were .14 and .04. Two cases Janis had proposed as groupthink, the Mayaguez rescue and the Iran hostage rescue, came out looking like the vigilant cases instead. Park ran the most complete single test. His abstract reports all 24 of the model's variables, 64 four-person ad hoc groups whose discussions were videotaped and content analysed, and Janis's predictions confirmed in only two of 23 cases. Mullen, Anthony, Salas and Driskell meta-analysed the cohesion prediction. Their abstract reports no significant effect of cohesiveness on decision quality overall, poorer decisions from cohesive groups when directive leadership was also present, and greater impairment the more a cohesion measure leaned on interpersonal attraction. Baron writes that their search found nine independent studies, and that the conditional result was marginally significant, r = -0.176, in three of seventeen experimental tests. Turner and Pratkanis summarise the early laboratory work the same way: studies of cohesion and leadership style show no adverse effect on performance, while instructing members to limit their discussion duly limited it. Hogg and Hains put 472 participants into four-person groups of friends, of socially attractive strangers or of random strangers, under background conditions for groupthink. Their abstract concludes that friendship was weakly and negatively related to the symptoms, and that identification and social attraction were strongly and mostly positively related. Baron's tabulation of their Table 1 does not read that way. Of 23 symptoms, group identification correlated positively with four at p of .05 or lower and one more at .08 or lower, and negatively with five. Baron adds in a footnote that the data do not support the claim made in their abstract. The clearest positive result is also secondhand here. Baron reports that Turner, Pratkanis, Probasco and Leve found threat of public scrutiny combined with high cohesion did lower decision quality, and that isolated studies of threat will not settle the question.

study.cite: Tetlock, P. E., Peterson, R. S., McGuire, C., Chang, S., & Feld, P. (1992). Assessing political group dynamics: A test of the groupthink model. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 63(3), 403-425.

replicated.weighting: standardised path from group cohesiveness to concurrence seeking in the strictly defined Janis model; the model's goodness of fit was .88 and its root mean square error .10

limits: Three of the figures on this page are quoted at one remove and are labelled in the text where they appear. Baron's count of nine studies in Mullen and colleagues, the r of -0.176 and its marginal significance, and the three of seventeen tests are Baron reporting them, not their own words; the Mullen abstract carries none of those numbers. Baron's own text was read from the author's preprint, while the citation names the published chapter in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, and those normally agree without being guaranteed to. The result attributed to Turner, Pratkanis, Probasco and Leve is Baron's description; their paper was not opened. Esser's full text is paywalled at ScienceDirect, so the counts of 11 laboratory studies and 17 historical reports come from Baron's reading of Esser, and the sentence quoted at page 133 from Baron's reproduction of it. The PubMed abstract was read and says none of those things. The previous version of this page said Park's 2000 abstract could not be obtained at the publisher, at Crossref or at Semantic Scholar. That was true of those three and wrong as a claim about the abstract, which is carried in full by OpenAlex from the publisher's deposit and was read there twice; Wiley's own page returns 403 and Park's full text was not opened. Henningsen and colleagues are cited from the abstract deposited at Crossref, which is why no sample size for that experiment appears above. Hogg and Hains give N as 472 without saying whether that is the number recruited or the number analysed, and their full text was not opened, so the page repeats the figure as printed. The search for later work covered Crossref, PubMed, archive.org, Open Library and general web search, and turned up no meta-analysis of the model after Mullen and colleagues in 1994 and no preregistered or multi-site replication of a groupthink experiment. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar answered single-record lookups on the day of this check but returned rate-limit errors on every search query, so neither index was searched. Effect sizes for the original are unavailable in principle, since the original is a set of historical case readings rather than a study. The Tetlock betas rest on 88 Q sorts from 10 episodes, which the authors themselves call marginally sufficient for the method.
misreadings: The word has come loose from the theory. Turner and Pratkanis note that it entered Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary by 1975, three years after the book, defined as conformity to group values and ethics. That is not what Janis proposed and not what the research tested. Cohesion is the second misreading. It is the antecedent everyone remembers and the one that keeps failing, and Janis himself wrote in 1972 that cohesiveness may be a necessary condition but is not a sufficient one. Tetlock and colleagues found it unrelated to concurrence seeking in the historical cases. Peterson and colleagues studied the top management teams of seven Fortune 500 companies, each at a successful and an unsuccessful moment, and found risk-taking, cohesion and strong opinionated leaders among the successful teams. The Bay of Pigs is the third. Kramer, working from declassified documents, oral histories and participants' memoirs, argues that much of the new evidence does not support Janis's characterisation, and that Kennedy and Johnson were weighing political costs rather than being carried by their groups. What survives the record is narrower than the name suggests. Directive leadership and organisational procedure predict poor decisions, which Baron notes would be expected even with no groupthink reactions at all. The neighbouring claims live elsewhere in this corpus and are not restated here: group polarisation is entry no. 267 and team error is entry no. 332.
